solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Band kit (5)

blocks.note: not a group of musicians but a long narrow piece of material
the matching outfit a sports team plays in

annotation.surface: Someone in a rock group asking about their gear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band kit' reads as a drum kit or a group's equipment. In British football a team's strip is its kit: the shirts, shorts and socks in club colours.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms: a narrow band of cloth, and the British word for a team's playing kit.

entries.clue: More surprisingly in support of article, mathematical statement (7)

indicatorNotes.surprisingly: MORE arranged surprisingly gives a new order
indicatorNotes.in support of: in a down answer, the part below supports the part above

annotation.surface: A mathematical statement turning out, more surprisingly, to back up an article.
annotation.walkthrough: 'More surprisingly' reads as a comparative adverb; split it into fodder and indicator. The anagram sits under the article in the grid, holding it up.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a statement in mathematics proved from axioms, like Pythagoras's.

entries.clue: I’ll take the food, but it’s unclear whether or not I care! (1,4,4,2,1,2)

annotation.answer: I DON'T MIND IF I DO
annotation.definition: I’ll take the food, but it’s unclear whether or not I care!

blocks.note: what the phrase actually means: a polite yes to an offer

blocks.clueFragment: but it’s unclear whether or not I care!
blocks.note: read literally, the words sound indifferent, as if the speaker could take it or leave it

annotation.surface: A guest accepting a second helping with mock reluctance.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is a stock British way to accept an offer, and the clue plays on how its literal words seem to say both 'I don't care' and 'yes please'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a polite acceptance whose literal wording sounds indifferent.

entries.clue: Remain behind for search (5)

indicatorNotes.behind: behind means following after, so the word for 'remain' comes after the word for 'for'

blocks.note: to be = to remain, as in 'let it be'

annotation.surface: Someone told to stay back and join a search party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Remain behind' wants to be a single phrase meaning stay late; it is a word plus a placement, and the order of the finished answer is the reverse of the clue's.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: as a noun, an investigation or searching inquiry.

entries.clue: Fast sheep, and a cuckoo (7)

indicatorNotes.cuckoo: cuckoo means crazy, so AND A is scrambled

blocks.note: a ram is a male sheep

annotation.surface: A speedy sheep and a cuckoo, like a farmyard race.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like a description of the sheep, but it is a noun: a period of going without food.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Muslim holy month of fasting.

entries.clue: Awful lot of money covering sport (9)

blocks.note: a mint = a lot of money, as in 'cost a mint'
on = covering, lying on top of

annotation.surface: Complaining about the huge sums spent on televising sport.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Covering' suggests media coverage of sport; here it simply means lying over something.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a racket game played with a shuttlecock over a net.

entries.clue: Substantial groom (4)

blocks.note: large, as in the informal phrase '___ sum'
a verb here: to make neat, not a bridegroom

annotation.surface: A well-built bridegroom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Groom' pairs with 'substantial' to suggest a hefty man at a wedding; it is a verb meaning make neat.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal adjective for a considerable amount, and a plain verb for making neat.

entries.clue: Sad bigmouth, not miserable sceptic (8,6)

indicatorNotes.miserable: miserable means in a sorry state, so the letters are out of order

annotation.surface: A sad loudmouth, not a miserable doubter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sad' and 'miserable' both look like indicators; 'sad' is fodder and 'miserable' does the work. The name comes from the apostle Thomas, who doubted the Resurrection.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from the Gospel of John: someone who refuses to believe without proof.

entries.clue: Uncover most of red meat (6)

indicatorNotes.most of: most of a word loses its last letter

annotation.surface: Lifting the cover off a plate of mostly red meat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Red meat' reads as one phrase, but the colour and the meat are separate pieces, and ironically this meat is pale.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to lay bare or make visible, as when lifting a lid.

entries.clue: Favouring one’s own spot, mine different (8)

indicatorNotes.different: SPOT MINE made different gives a new arrangement of its letters

annotation.surface: Someone choosing their own spot over another's and insisting theirs is different.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition leaves the object unsaid: 'one's own' means one's own relatives. The comma between 'spot' and 'mine' only serves the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: the practice of giving jobs and favours to one's own family.

entries.clue: Mover of animals, dog behind shepherd’s back (6)

indicatorNotes.back: the back of a word is its last letter
indicatorNotes.behind: behind means following after, so the dog's name comes after the shepherd's last letter

blocks.note: Rover is the stock name for a dog

annotation.surface: A sheepdog trotting along behind the shepherd as the flock is moved.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface places the dog behind the shepherd himself; the wordplay puts it behind only his last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: one who drives cattle or sheep to market, moving animals for a living.

entries.clue: Quite delightful (6)

blocks.note: an adverb meaning fairly or rather, as in '___ good'
an adjective meaning pleasing to look at

annotation.walkthrough: The two words read as one phrase of mild praise, but each is a separate definition: an adverb and an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: One word serving as both an informal adverb for 'fairly' and an adjective for attractive.

entries.clue: Winger on the turn, drained, moved with the ball (8)

blocks.note: a bird is a winged creature
bled = drained, as a radiator or a patient

annotation.surface: A football winger cutting inside, running out of energy as he carries the ball forward.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Winger' is set up as a wide football player, which fits the ball perfectly; here it is just something with wings.
annotation.definitionFit: A football term: carrying the ball forward with small, repeated touches of the foot.

entries.clue: Wet items on ground (7)

indicatorNotes.ground: ground means crushed and broken up, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Things left lying outside on damp ground.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' belongs to the fodder, not a link word. 'Wet' is a verb here, to match the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, taking 'Wet' as a verb: to make damp.

entries.clue: Serious player, and great I suspect (9)

indicatorNotes.suspect: suspect means dubious, so the letters are unreliable in order

annotation.surface: An earnest actor who suspects he is great.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' is part of the fodder, not a link. 'I suspect' reads as an aside; only 'suspect' is the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful description: an actor in tragedies plays serious parts, and 'player' is an old word for actor.

entries.clue: Chicken feed, sweet (6)

blocks.note: not grain for hens but an idiom for a paltry sum of money
in Britain, the dessert course, here one layered with sponge, fruit, custard and cream

annotation.surface: What to give the hens, and a treat afterwards.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chicken feed' reads literally as poultry grain but means a paltry amount. In Britain 'sweet' is also a pudding, and trifle is a classic one.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for something negligible, and a definition by example of a British dessert.

entries.clue: Amphitheatres where charity at stake originally, looking back (6)

indicatorNotes.originally: the origin of 'stake' is its first letter
indicatorNotes.looking back: the assembled string is read backwards

blocks.note: aid = charity, help for those in need

annotation.surface: Big arenas where a charity event has money riding on it.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole string AIDATS is reversed at once, not each piece in place. The Latin plural is the one needed to fit six letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: arenas ringed with tiered seats, as Roman amphitheatres were.

entries.clue: Bug in jar, not spreadable (6)

indicatorNotes.spreadable: the letters can be spread out and rearranged

annotation.surface: An insect found in a jar of something that is not spreadable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bug' suggests an insect; it is computer malware.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose computing sense: malicious software disguised as harmless, named after the Trojan horse.

entries.clue: Country roads seen after turning around for example (7)

indicatorNotes.turning: LANES turned back to front reads SENAL
indicatorNotes.around: around means surrounding, so the turned roads enclose the abbreviation

blocks.note: surface padding: the roads are simply seen once turned

annotation.surface: Country roads spotted after someone turns round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country roads' reads as one rural phrase, but 'Country' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a nation in West Africa.

entries.clue: Colonist, bill payer? (7)

blocks.note: one who makes a home in new territory
one who pays off what is owed, a whimsical coinage

annotation.surface: A colonist handed the bill.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented sense: one who settles a bill.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a colonist, and a literal reading of 'one who settles' an account.

entries.clue: Line ending novel I alter, exactly as read (7)

indicatorNotes.novel: novel means new, so I ALTER is rearranged
indicatorNotes.ending: 'Line ending' means the line forms the ending of what follows, so L comes last

annotation.surface: Changing the last line of a novel so it reads exactly right.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as a book but is the anagram indicator; 'Line ending' reads as the last line of that book.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain sense: taking words in their exact, word-for-word meaning.

entries.clue: Bed into which female snuggles in new semi, most cosy (8)

indicatorNotes.into which: 'into which' says the rest is put inside the bed
indicatorNotes.snuggles in: to snuggle in is to nestle inside, so F sits within the rearranged SEMI

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
rearranged to MIES, with F put after the M

annotation.surface: A woman curled up in bed in her new semi-detached house, as snug as can be.
annotation.walkthrough: A semi is a British semi-detached house. There are two layers of containment: F into rearranged SEMI, then all of that into the bed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the superlative of the informal 'comfy', which means cosy.

entries.clue: Island a success in heart of nation (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' says the success sits inside the letters that follow
indicatorNotes.heart of: the heart of a word is its middle letters

annotation.surface: An island that has become a success at the heart of a nation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heart of nation' takes two letters, not one, because the word has an even number of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the largest island of French Polynesia.

entries.clue: Minute, little time during year (4)

annotation.surface: A minute is a little bit of time within a year.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minute' looks like a unit of time, which the rest of the clue backs up; it is the adjective pronounced my-NEWT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym once 'minute' is read as the adjective meaning extremely small.

entries.clue: Indian leader with leader from Hungary embraced by soldier (6)

indicatorNotes.from: 'leader from' asks for the first letter, the one at the front
indicatorNotes.embraced by: to be embraced is to be held inside someone's arms, so AND H sits inside the soldier

annotation.surface: An Indian leader, and a Hungarian one, hugged by a soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leader' appears twice: first as part of the definition, then as a first-letter instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Mahatma Gandhi led India's independence movement.

entries.clue: Get stamp showing well-known monument, say (8)

blocks.note: to land = to get, as in 'land a job'
a mark = a stamp or imprint

annotation.surface: Buying a postage stamp that shows a famous monument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stamp' suggests a postage stamp; it is just a mark. 'Say' warns that a monument is only one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a famous monument is one kind of prominent feature that identifies a place.

entries.clue: Idle rejection of piece from Sartre, nihilistic (5)

indicatorNotes.rejection of: a rejection throws the piece back, so it reads backwards
indicatorNotes.piece from: the letters are a piece taken from the words that follow

annotation.surface: A philosopher's rejection of Sartre's nihilism as idle talk.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters span the two words, jumping the comma. Sartre and nihilism fit together because Sartre was an existentialist philosopher.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: not moving or acting, inactive.

entries.clue: Odd bits forgotten in opus sadly, my song (5)

indicatorNotes.Odd bits forgotten: drop the odd-numbered letters, keeping the even ones

blocks.note: even letters of oPuS sAdLy My

annotation.surface: A composer lamenting that bits of their opus were forgotten.
annotation.walkthrough: Count across 'opus sadly my' as one string: O P U S S A D L Y M Y, keeping letters 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a sacred song, as in the Book of Psalms.
